abstract_sentences.text: Current motion-conditioned video generation methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction.

evidence.anchor: current; prohibitive latency; minutes per video

abstract_sentences.text: We present MotionStream, enabling sub-second latency with up to 29 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.

evidence.anchor: sub-second; up to 29 FPS; single GPU

abstract_sentences.text: Our approach begins by augmenting a text-to-video model with motion control, which generates high-quality videos that adhere to the global text prompt and local motion guidance, but does not perform inference on the fly.

evidence.anchor: global text prompt; local motion guidance; no on-the-fly inference

abstract_sentences.text: As such, we distill this bidirectional teacher into a causal student through Self Forcing with Distribution Matching Distillation, enabling real-time streaming inference.

evidence.anchor: Self Forcing; Distribution Matching Distillation; causal student

abstract_sentences.text: Several key challenges arise when generating videos of long, potentially infinite time-horizons -- (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to infinite horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without incurring growth in computational cost due to increasing context windows.

evidence.anchor: three challenges: finite-to-infinite, error accumulation, context growth

abstract_sentences.text: A key to our approach is introducing carefully designed sliding-window causal attention, combined with attention sinks.

evidence.anchor: sliding-window causal attention; attention sinks

abstract_sentences.text: By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we properly simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos.

evidence.anchor: self-rollout; KV cache rolling; fixed context window

abstract_sentences.text: Our models achieve state-of-the-art results in motion following and video quality while being two orders of magnitude faster, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming.

evidence.anchor: state-of-the-art; two orders of magnitude faster; infinite-length

abstract_sentences.text: With MotionStream, users can paint trajectories, control cameras, or transfer motion, and see results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.

evidence.anchor: paint trajectories; control cameras; transfer motion; real-time
The ultimate goal of motion-controlled video synthesis is to give creators the power of a director’s chair.
The promise of interactive control is currently hindered by several fundamental constraints.
To overcome these challenges, we introduce MotionStream, a method designed specifically for an interactive creative experience.
Our approach starts with a motion-controlled teacher model that uses lightweight sinusoidal embeddings.
MotionStream achieves 17 FPS at 480P and 10 FPS at 720P resolutions with sub-second latency.
Our key contributions are: 1. We present the first streaming motion-conditioned video generation pipeline.
Controllable Video Generation groups structure, camera, subject, audio, and motion control.
Full bidirectional attention requires the entire control signal to be known in advance.
Autoregressive Video Models moves from GANs to diffusion/AR and AR-diffusion hybrids.
Recent teacher-to-AR distillation can drift beyond the training horizon or require long-video finetuning.

final_judgment.single_storyline: A lightweight motion-conditioned bidirectional teacher is distilled with joint guidance into a causal student; rolling KV cache, attention sinks, a fixed local window, and Tiny VAE connect quality, long-horizon stability, and interactive speed. Evidence p.4–p.7 and p.9.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The body retains Eq. (1)–(4), the teacher/student pipeline, Tables 1–4, Figures 3–8, default c3s1w1 and wt=3.0/wm=1.5, plus FPS/latency. Evidence p.4–p.10.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Tiny VAE training, VBench/user study, extended ablations, training details, evaluation protocols, failure cases, ethics, and reproducibility are moved to Appendix A–G. Evidence p.19–p.26.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 2 previews the pipeline, Figure 3 turns attention observation into a mechanism, Table 4/Figure 6 test drift, and Eq. (1)/(2) pair with Table 3/Figures 4–5 for local method-to-evidence links. Evidence p.4–p.9.
final_judgment.largest_gap: Infinite-length, first, state-of-the-art, and two-orders-of-magnitude wording exceeds the directly bounded evidence. Extrapolation reaches 241 frames and comparisons use selected baselines without uncertainty. Evidence p.7–p.9 and p.25.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For each real-time system claim, report fixed-hardware throughput/latency, quality cost, long-horizon curves, component deletion, and callable training/evaluation matching details. This rule is grounded in p.7–p.9 and p.22–p.25.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: The rule fits generation systems with speed-quality-stability tradeoffs. Pure-theory or static-quality papers need different falsifiable objects rather than FPS/latency evidence. This boundary is an interpretation of the evidence in p.4–p.9.
